text.p: Monterey Resources Inc, California's largest heavy oil producer, is considering more acquisitions following last week's buyout of McFarland Energy Inc, chief executive Graham Whaling said in an interview.

"If (oil) prices rebound we might consider taking on more leverage...We've got a couple candidates in mind but I wouldn't want to disclose them (apart from saying) they'd be in California," Whaling said.

Last week's buyout adds 20 million barrels of oil equivalent to Monterey's 218 million proven reserves and will help boost its daily output by 4,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) to 51,000 bpd, or five percent of California's total, by year end.

Earlier this year, Whaling said his company would also look into overseas ventures with heavy oil producers in western Canada and Venezuela. In the interview he added that a foreign deal was at least a year away and would follow local acquisitions.
"We want to stick with the California heavy oil business," he said.

To help improve cash flow, especially given the drop in California heavy crude oil prices to around $13.50 a barrel currently from average $16 in the first quarter, the company plans to increase production and cut costs, Whaling said.
Operating costs in the first half were between $3.55 and $3.60 a barrel. "We expect to bring that down over the remainder of the year," he said, without quantifying.

Monterey also will try to make more money by accelerating its drilling and steam injection program, hoping to increase daily production a total of 10 percent by mid-1998 from its current level of about 47,000 bpd.
Cost savings could come from the former McFarland oil fields, where steam can be injected from nearby Monterey properties and oil output boosted.
For the remainder of 1997, the company plans to drill 44 expensive but high-yielding horizontal wells. Two lie on McFarland properlty contiguous to Monterey's highest producing wells.

It also plans to increase the amount of steam injection into McFarland's former properties, Whaling said. The company hopes to lift their production to 4,000 bpd this year, and increase ouput to 4,600 bpd next year.
The accelerated use of steam will require more purchases of natural gas to generate it, something the company found costly earlier this year, when prices rose.
Monterey had hoped to acquire 20 million cubic feet a day (mcf/d) in natural gas, but with the McFarland property holding just five mcf, more money will be spent, Whaling said.
"We'll just have to purchase increased volumes of natural gas," Whaling said. He estimated the company will spend an $180,000 a month to buy the extra 3 mcf/d of natural gas.
But Whaling hopes California crude oil prices will find support or even firm later this year because West Coast refining capacity vastly outrips production.
"We dont' expect (the price) to weaken," he said. The supply/demand relationship on the West Coast is tight."
